idiom_name: Operation subclass + OperationQueue (+ UndoManager), or actor + AsyncStream
implementation_notes: Foundation supplies the pattern nearly whole: an `Operation` subclass is the concrete command (it encapsulates the request and exposes `main()`, `cancel()`, dependencies, `qualityOfService` and completion), and `OperationQueue` is the concrete processor - `maxConcurrentOperationCount`, `isSuspended`, dependencies and QoS are the scheduling policy, `addOperation` is the submit call, and `UndoManager` implements the undo service. `BlockOperation` covers trivial closure-shaped commands. The Swift-concurrency form of the same roles is an `actor` (which serialises execution) fed by an `AsyncStream` (the queue, bounded via its buffering policy) plus a `TaskGroup` for parallel dispatch; prefer it in new code, but keep OperationQueue when dependencies, cancelling and progress reporting are needed off the shelf.
pitfalls: Cancellation is cooperative: an Operation that never checks isCancelled keeps running, and the queue only marks it cancelled.
Operation subclasses re-entering mutable state from several queue threads need synchronisation; Operations are not automatically Sendable.
OperationQueue.waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished() on the main thread deadlocks the UI; use completion blocks or async/await with a TaskGroup instead.
UndoManager registers undo per run-loop group: commands executed off the main run loop must call beginUndoGrouping/endUndoGrouping explicitly or their inverse lands in the wrong group.
An AsyncStream with an unbounded buffering policy removes the backpressure the queue was meant to provide.
